hints: Break down the name ethanedioic acid, the ethane part tells you the carbon chain length and the dioic acid part tells you how many carboxyl groups are present and where they are.
walkthrough:
Decode the name**
Think of yourself building from the name. Ethane means a two carbon chain, and dioic acid means there are two carboxylic acid groups, one at each end. So you do not have a hydrocarbon chain with substituents, you simply have two $\text{-COOH}$ groups joined directly together.

Draw every bond**
A displayed formula must show every atom and every bond. Draw $\text{H-O-}$ single bonded to a $\text{C}$, that $\text{C}$ double bonded to $\text{O}$ and single bonded to the second $\text{C}$, and mirror this on the other side to give $\text{H-O-C(=O)-C(=O)-O-H}$. Check you have $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{2}\text{O}_{4}$ in total.
Final answer: Displayed formula showing $\text{HO-C(=O)-C(=O)-OH}$ with all bonds shown: H-O-C(=O)-C(=O)-O-H, each C bonded to one OH and double bonded to one O.

hints: Compare structures, methanoic acid $\text{HCOOH}$ contains H-C=O like an aldehyde, propanoic acid $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COOH}$ does not, and ethanedioic acid $\text{HOOC-COOH}$ has two carboxyl groups joined together.
Recall which mild oxidising reagents give a positive test only with aldehydes and therefore also with methanoic acid, but not with other carboxylic acids.
Recall which strong purple oxidising agent is decolourised when it oxidises a reducing agent, and think about which of these three acids can act as reducing agents.
Use the logic that one reagent should pick out methanoic acid alone, while the second reagent should pick out both methanoic and ethanedioic acids, leaving propanoic acid negative to both.
walkthrough:
Spot the special reducing group**
Look closely at methanoic acid, $\text{H-C(=O)-OH}$. It has a hydrogen attached directly to the carbonyl carbon, just like an aldehyde $\text{R-CHO}$. That H can be oxidised to $\text{CO}_{2}$ and water. Propanoic acid $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COOH}$ has no such H, so it resists oxidation. Ethanedioic acid $\text{HOOC-COOH}$ is also easily oxidised to $2\text{CO}_{2}$, but it does not have aldehyde character.

Choose a mild aldehyde test for reagent 1**
Fehling's solution (blue $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ complex) or Tollens' reagent ($[\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_{3})_{2}]^{+}$) are mild oxidants that only oxidise aldehydes under normal conditions. So only methanoic acid will react. With Fehling's heated you get a brick-red precipitate of $\text{Cu}_{2}\text{O}$, with Tollens' you get a silver mirror of $\text{Ag}$. Propanoic acid and ethanedioic acid show no change, the solution stays blue with Fehling's.

Choose a strong oxidant for reagent 2**
Acidified potassium manganate(VII), $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}$, purple, is a powerful oxidant. It will oxidise both reducing acids, methanoic acid and ethanedioic acid, itself being reduced from $\text{Mn(VII)}$ purple to $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ colourless. Propanoic acid cannot be oxidised this way, so the purple colour remains.

Build the distinguishing table**
Now you have full separation. Propanoic acid: negative to both. Methanoic acid: positive to both. Ethanedioic acid: negative to Fehling's / Tollens' but positive to acidified $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}$. That combination of two tests uniquely identifies all three.

Final answer: reagent 1: Fehling's reagent (or Tollens' reagent); reagent 2: acidified $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}$ (acidified $\text{KMnO}_{4}$).
propanoic acid: no change / stays blue with reagent 1, stays purple with reagent 2.
methanoic acid: red / brick-red precipitate with Fehling's (or silver mirror with Tollens'), purple to colourless with reagent 2.
ethanedioic acid: no change with reagent 1, purple to colourless with reagent 2.

hints: Compare structures, propanoic acid is $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COOH}$ while 2,2-dichloropropanoic acid is $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CCl}_{2}\text{COOH}$, focus on what the two Cl atoms replace and how electronegative Cl is compared to H.

Think about acid dissociation $\text{HA} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^{+} + \text{A}^{-}$ and how pulling electron density away from the $\text{O-H}$ bond and from the $\text{COO}^{-}$ group affects dissociation and anion stability.
walkthrough:
Picture the structural difference**
Write them side by side. Propanoic acid is $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{-COOH}$. In 2,2-dichloropropanoic acid it is $\text{CH}_{3}\text{-CCl}_{2}\text{-COOH}$, so two H atoms on C-2 (the carbon next to the $\text{COOH}$) are replaced by two Cl atoms. Chlorine is far more electronegative than hydrogen or carbon.

Follow the electron pull**
Those Cl atoms pull electron density towards themselves through the sigma bonds, the negative inductive (-I) effect. This pulls electrons away from the carboxyl group. That has two linked consequences: the $\text{O-H}$ bond in $\text{-COOH}$ becomes more polar and weaker, so $\text{H}^{+}$ is released more easily, and once lost, the negative charge on the carboxylate $\text{-COO}^{-}$ is spread out and stabilised by the electron withdrawing Cl atoms. A more stable conjugate base means a stronger acid, so $$\text{CH}_{3}\text{CCl}_{2}\text{COOH} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_{3}\text{CCl}_{2}\text{COO}^{-} + \text{H}^{+}$$ lies further to the right than for propanoic acid.

Final answer: Cl atoms are strongly electronegative / electron withdrawing by the inductive effect.
They withdraw electron density from the $\text{O-H}$ bond, weakening it and favouring $\text{H}^{+}$ loss, and stabilise the $\text{CCl}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}\text{COO}^{-}$ conjugate base by dispersing the negative charge.
